lesson.title: Extremes and Totals: min, max, and sum
lesson.summary: The built-in functions min(), max(), and sum() scan an entire list in one call to find the smallest value, the largest value, or the total of all values, saving you from writing that loop by hand.
lesson.body:
Lists frequently hold numeric data: test scores, temperatures, prices, distances. Three built-in functions handle the most common questions you would otherwise answer with a hand-written loop and an accumulator variable. min(mylist) returns the smallest element, max(mylist) returns the largest, and sum(mylist) returns the total of all elements added together.

```python
temps = [68, 72, 65, 80, 74]
print(min(temps))
print(max(temps))
print(sum(temps))
print(sum(temps) / len(temps))
```

This prints 65, then 80, then 359, then 71.8. The first three come straight from scanning the list once: the coldest reading is 65, the warmest is 80, and all five values add up to 359. The last line combines sum with len, the function you will look at next, to compute an average, one of the single most common patterns you will write in this course: sum divided by count.

sum accepts an optional second argument, a starting value to add before it begins, which is occasionally useful when you want to add a list's total onto some existing running total: sum([1, 2, 3], 100) returns 106. Without that second argument, sum defaults to starting from 0, which is why sum([1, 2, 3]) alone returns 6.

A caution worth internalizing early: min, max, and sum all rely on being able to compare or add the elements to each other, so every element in the list needs to be a compatible type. sum on a list of strings does not concatenate them, it raises a TypeError, because Python's sum defaults to adding onto the integer 0, and 0 plus a string is not defined. If you truly want to join a list of strings together, the tool for that is ''.join(mylist), not sum. Likewise, calling min or max on a list that mixes numbers and strings, like [3, 'cat', 5], raises a TypeError, because Python 3 refuses to guess whether a string is less than or greater than a number. These functions are powerful precisely because they assume the list is internally consistent; keeping your lists to one type of data, a habit you should already be building, is what keeps min, max, and sum reliable.
